explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Moses says the judges are to judge the people "…with righteous judgment." Not fast judgment, not popular judgment, righteous. A judge who rules on mood is just a person with a hunch and a nice chair.
I see why you'd go there, since the judges are appointed for the tribes. But the standard Moses gives isn't custom. It's righteous judgment. The same measuring stick in every town, and I like that.

Whatever the town decides sounds a lot like a group chat picking a movie. Forty minutes later, still no movie. Moses gives a clearer standard: the judges are to judge the people with righteous judgment. Nobody has to take a vote on that.

explanations.answer: Blinds their eyes and twists their words
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says "…a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous." Notice who he's talking about: the wise and the righteous. If it can get to them, nobody should think they're too sharp for it.

explanations.answer: Makes them rich and then makes them lazy
explanations.explanation: Moses never says anything about getting rich or lazy. What he says is that a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise. The trouble is what it does to their seeing, not what it does to their schedule.

explanations.answer: Turns their whole town against them
explanations.explanation: The town doesn't come into this one, friend. Moses says a bribe "…twists the words of the righteous." It goes after their sight and their speech. Two things get hit, and neither one is the neighbors.

Right on the money, friend. Moses says to pursue justice so that they may live and possess the land the LORD their God is giving them. Notice it says giving. It's a gift they're walking into. And justice, and justice alone, is how they're to live in it.
No temple in this verse, friend. Moses is talking about the land the LORD their God is giving them. An altar comes up in the very next verse, but a temple never does. Stay with the land.

A king does come up later in this passage, so I get why your mind went there. But in this verse, Moses says the people are to possess the land. Kingdom talk waits for Deuteronomy 17:14. One thing at a time.

Yes! Moses says, "…do not set up for yourselves a sacred pillar, which the LORD your God hates." That's a strong word, and it's right there in the verse. It sits right beside the Asherah pole, so he's closing the door on both.

A golden calf, friend? I love the confidence. I once stamped a whole batch with the wrong shape and kept going like nothing happened, so I know that feeling. But this verse names a sacred pillar, and it says the LORD your God hates it. Moses has the Asherah pole in the verse right before, and the pillar is the one that follows.
Close to the neighborhood, but not the house. The verse names a sacred pillar, and it adds that the LORD your God hates it. No carved idol in this one. Just the pillar.
True, baker. Moses says not to sacrifice to the LORD an ox or a sheep "…with any defect or serious flaw…" He calls that detestable to the LORD your God. The offering is supposed to be a good one.
It's the other way around, friend. Moses says you shall not sacrifice an ox or a sheep with any defect or serious flaw. He calls that detestable to the LORD your God. So the statement was true.
That's right. Moses says, "…you must investigate it thoroughly." A report is only a report until somebody checks. And thoroughly means all the way, not a quick peek.
Hold on, friend. A report isn't the same as proof. Moses says, "…you must investigate it thoroughly." The punishment only comes into it if the report is true.

explanations.answer: Send them out of the land
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that here, friend. First comes the checking: "…you must investigate it thoroughly." Then he says what to do if the report is true. Sending anybody anywhere isn't the first step.

Yes, baker. Moses says, "On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death…" This is a heavy part, and the rule is careful for a reason I think we can feel. One voice alone is never enough.
Moses shuts that down. He says a man "…shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness." One voice isn't enough, even a trusted one. It takes two or three.
Twelve is a whole tour bus of witnesses, friend. Moses asks for less than that: two or three witnesses. And he's firm that a lone witness isn't enough. So the number sits between one and a crowd.

explanations.answer: The place the LORD will choose
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, "…you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose." Notice he doesn't name the place yet. The LORD does the choosing, and the people do the going.

Cities of refuge do come up in Moses' speech, friend (Deuteronomy 4:41–43), but this verse doesn't send a hard case there. Moses says you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose, and then you go to the Levitical priests and the judge who presides at that time (Deuteronomy 17:8–9). Picture taking your hard case to the wrong building. You wait in line, get all the way to the window, and hear "wrong department." Check the address first, baker.

Closest isn't the rule here, friend. Moses says you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose. It's about where the LORD points, not what's on the map nearby. A big wall doesn't make a big answer.
Yes, baker. Moses says to go "…to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time." Both of them together, priests and judge. That's who gives the verdict.

Elders are a fair guess, friend. I'd have guessed them too if I were rushing. But Moses says to go to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time. Priests and a judge, side by side. Then, he says, "Inquire of them, and they will give you a verdict in the case."
Scribes don't show up in this verse, friend. Moses sends them to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time. They inquire, and the priests and the judge give the verdict.
Moses says the opposite, friend. He says, "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you." No little tweaks and no personal edits. So the statement was false.

False is right. Moses says, "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you." That leaves no room for a little adjustment. You don't get to edit the verdict because you'd have written it differently.

explanations.answer: He must be put to death
explanations.explanation: Yes, and I'll say it plain: this one is heavy. Moses says the man who acts presumptuously and refuses to listen to the priest or the judge "…must be put to death." He adds, "You must purge the evil from Israel." It's a serious thing to refuse the verdict.

explanations.answer: He pays a fine to the priests
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't mention a fine, friend. He says the man who refuses to listen to the priest or the judge must be put to death. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously. He adds that they must purge the evil from Israel.

explanations.answer: He is sent out of the town
explanations.explanation: Nothing about being sent out of town in this one. Moses says the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to listen to the priest or the judge, must be put to death. I think this is a hard line to read. But that's what the verse says.

True, baker. Moses says, "Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly." The whole people hear about it, and it shapes how they act. Verse 13 is easy to skim past when the verses right before it are so heavy. I'd say it's worth slowing down for.

That one was true, friend. Moses says, "Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly." It's right there in verse 13. Easy to miss when the verses before it are so heavy.
Yes. Moses says, "…you are to appoint over yourselves the king whom the LORD your God shall choose." Israel does the appointing, but the choosing belongs to the LORD. Even the king is picked by Him.
Elders are a sensible guess, but the verse doesn't name them. Moses says the king is the one "…whom the LORD your God shall choose." The choice isn't a committee's. It's the LORD's.
The priests do show up later when the king writes his scroll. But they aren't the ones choosing. Moses says the king is the one "…whom the LORD your God shall choose." That's the whole answer.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, "you are not to set over yourselves a foreigner who is not one of your brothers." There's no clause about being a strong leader. The king comes from among their brothers, full stop.

False is right. Moses says, "Appoint a king from among your brothers; you are not to set over yourselves a foreigner who is not one of your brothers." No strong leader exception is in there. The line is drawn plainly.

explanations.answer: The LORD said never go back that way
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Moses says, "…for the LORD has said, ‘You are never to go back that way again.’" The king must not acquire many horses for himself, and he must not send the people back to Egypt to get more. The reason Moses gives for that second part is what the LORD said.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh won't sell horses to Israel
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh, Egypt's king, doesn't come into this verse at all. Moses gives a different reason: the LORD has said, "You are never to go back that way again." The text doesn't say anything about what Egypt would or wouldn't sell. Stick to what the LORD said.

explanations.answer: The road there is far too dangerous
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about the road being dangerous, friend. The reason Moses gives is what the LORD has said: "You are never to go back that way again." I'd rather you remember it his way.
Yes, heart. Moses says the king must not take many wives for himself, "…lest his heart go astray." It's the heart he's watching over. Not the throne and not the treasury.
The army is a fair guess, since we just talked horses. But Moses says the king must not take many wives for himself, "…lest his heart go astray." It's the heart that could go astray.
The people matter in this passage, but not in this line. Moses says the king must not take many wives for himself, "…lest his heart go astray." It's the king's heart on the line.
Moses says the opposite. "He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold." A king with a big pile is the exact picture he's warning about. So the statement was false.

False is right. Moses says the king "…must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold." He's got a list of things the king can't stack up: horses, wives, and now silver and gold. That's a king who has to hold things loosely.

explanations.answer: All the days of his life
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The scroll "…is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life…" Not a one-time read and then onto the shelf. Every day for as long as he lives.
The first year would be a nice start, but Moses asks for far more. He says the king is to read from it "…all the days of his life…" That's a long time to keep a scroll close.
Peace isn't a stopping point in this verse. Moses says the king is to read from it "…all the days of his life…" There's no finish line except the end of his days.

That's it. Moses says the king reads "…so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes." Reading and keeping the words go together. That's how the learning happens.
Speaking for the LORD isn't what the verse says. Moses says the king reads "…so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God…" Learning to fear Him is the goal.
Teaching isn't mentioned here, friend. The king reads so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God. He's the student in this verse, and the scroll is his lesson.

True, baker. The king is to write himself a copy of the instruction and read from it all the days of his life, "…so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes." (Deuteronomy 17:19). Then Moses says, "…his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen…" (Deuteronomy 17:20). So the scroll isn't just for owning, it's for learning and observing. A king who copies it by hand and keeps coming back to it? That's a king getting his heart humbled one page at a time.

That one was true, friend. Moses says, "Then his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen…" That follows right after the king keeps the instruction on his scroll. It's the opposite of what you picked.

explanations.answer: He and his sons reign many years
explanations.explanation: Yes! Moses says it's "…in order that he and his sons may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel." Notice his sons are in there too. Keeping the instruction touches more than just the king.

explanations.answer: He never loses a single battle
explanations.explanation: That's a big promise, and Moses doesn't make it. What he says is that the king and his sons "…may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel." Battles don't come up here. It's about years on the throne.

Growing borders sound nice, but Moses doesn't say that. He says it's so that the king and his sons "…may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel." The purpose he gives is about years on the throne. Land getting bigger isn't in the verse.
